title: Exit codes
subtitle: Bash status numbers, $?, and what each code means

cards.meaning: Integer 0–255 that every command (and every script) finishes with
cards.notes: By convention 0 means success; non-zero means failure.
Memory hook: 0 = OK. Anything else = look up why.
Any status other than 0 signals failure; specific numbers carry more detail.

cards.meaning: Exit status of the last command
cards.notes: The shell stores the previous command’s status here. Range 0–255.

cards.meaning: Print the exit status of the previous command
cards.notes: Read it right after the command — the next command overwrites $?.

cards.meaning: exit takes only integer args in the range 0–255
cards.notes: exit is a byte. Negative values and fractions are not legal arguments.
Miscellaneous errors, such as divide by zero and other impermissible operations. If notes give no more specific number, think 1.
Missing keyword or command, or permission problem (and diff return code on a failed binary file comparison).
Permission problem or command is not an executable. Name resolved — kernel will not run it. Memory hook: 126 = found it, cannot run it.
Possible problem with $PATH or a typo. Memory hook: 127 = never found it.

cards.meaning: 126 = found a file but cannot run it; 127 = no command was found
cards.notes: 126: name resolved, not executable / permission. 127: typo or $PATH missing the directory.
exit takes only integer args in the range 0–255 (a fraction is invalid).
$? is 128 plus the signal number. Memory hook: 128+n = killed by signal n.
Control-C is fatal error signal 2 (SIGINT). 130 = 128 + 2. Memory hook: Ctrl-C = SIGINT = signal 2 → 130.
exit takes only integer args in the range 0–255. A negative argument produces out-of-range status 255.
